Question: On May 29, the Office of the US Trade Representative held a hearing on the 301 investigation of China's maritime, logistics and shipbuilding industries, and many parties opposed the imposition of tariffs before the meeting. What do you think?
Answer: The problem is the remedy proposed, which is the imposition of a docking fee in all US port of calls, targeting China-built ships exclusively. The remedy aims to collect at least $1m per ship docking (calibrated to the cost of goods carried) to feed a fund benefiting shipbuilding and metalworking unions. That’s robbing Peter to pay Paul, and unprecedented. It is also illegal, because of the brazen, targeted nature, just like the blanket tariffs announced under Donald. That is why the WTO’s dispute settlement mechanism remains paralyzed. This is also a tariff on tariff for goods originating from China carried on board China-built ships, because of the blanket tariff already in place. Where is this going to end? Are they going after China-built containers next, imposing a handling fee for every container based on cost of goods carried? I won’t be surprised if this passes, because America is willing to throw in the kitchen sink just to “win”. It will stop at nothing, not even general war. Is it a good idea, economically? No, because it will reshape trade flow, while China-built ships maintain a healthy economic edge over rivals. It just adds to the cost of doing business with the US, making the consumer pay more to benefit the pockets of a small number of union workers, funding the retirement of baby boomers. There is no way to revitalize ocean-going shipbuilding stateside with the cost structure today. The Jones Act, after all, dates back to 1920, and what has a century of protectionism bought?

Question: Are you convinced by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's argument that the ringgit's decline does not reflect the reality of Malaysia's strengthening economy?
Answer: That’s a departure from Mahathir’s horror almost 30 years ago, when he complained loudly about the currency turmoil during the AFC that WIPED OUT TWO DECADES OF GROWTH IN TWO WEEKS, with Malaysia losing billions in purchasing power. The devaluation of the ringgit is structural and has been ongoing for 4 decades. In 1980, Singapore was still in a currency union with Malaysia. The SGD was 1:1 with the MYR. Today, it is >3.5, the lowest it has ever been. Is it a floor? I don’t think so. Malaysia is styling itself as a cheaper alternative to China in some sectors, and growth has mostly been padded by forex, particularly the reverse plaza accord over the past decade. Otherwise, the Malaysia today is not too different from the Malaysia of the 2000s, competitive advantage wise. Is Malaysia climbing out of covid? Certainly. But is it clawing back lost decades? I don’t see it. Put another way, can Malaysia grow in an appreciating ringgit environment? I welcome being proven wrong, but I’m not optimistic, given the feedback from the grapevine.

Question: Did the U.S. Commerce Department tech sanctions on China spark the fall in Intel’s share price and decision to lay off 15k employees?
Answer: Well, dell is on course to lay off 25k staff this year and last. Dell's employee count is in the same low 100k bracket as Intel. Evidently, there has been a huge squeeze on the x86 ecosystem the past 2 years. My friend recently returned from a stateside trip to survey investment opportunities. I asked him about Intel and he said it wasn't on his shortlist of blue chip picks. His homework? Go through the Financials. Here're some numbers. Intel's revenue is down 30% last year compared to the pandemic driven peak of 2020-2021. That's a 24b hole. Now, the US GDP was 20t in 2017. Last year, it was 27t, a 35% increase, with a big chunk of it inflation driven. The problem for Intel? It brought in less revenue in 2023 compared to 2017! Intel has a peculiar way of reporting geographical revenue. It divides the pie into 5 parts. China, US, rest of the world, Singapore and Taiwan, sorted for size. Intel sells 3x as many chips to China, Singapore and Taiwan compared to the rest of the world ex-US. Surprised? The problem with Intel is structural, and it goes to the heart of the business model. Intel is vertically integrated. It is not only a chip designer, it is also a chip fabricator. Whereas everyone else is fabless today, and the list includes Nvidia, qualcomm and apple. Intel used to have defacto control of chipmaking tools and marerials, because it had the biggest budget at the head of the x86 monopoly. Unfortunately, the iPhone and arm changed the status quo irrevocably. Revenue from Apple and Android supercharged the contract manufacturing of chips, and within 6-8 years of the iphone's introduction, tsmc overhauled intel's lead as the owner of the leading edge process node. The best chipmaking tools were now offered to tsmc and Samsung, as Intel failed to find its lost mojo. There are reports of abnormal processor failure rates in the latest 13th and 14th generation products, which have affected the revenue of system builders. Promises made in the past few years by management regarding tech leadership and expansion have fallen flat. All told, it is a tale of a company in crisis, and cost cutting mode, rather than the confident growth of a company enabled by CHIPS act grants and loans. Now back to China. The Chinese government has ordered all departments to transition away from Microsoft and Intel products, due to the growing risk of sanctions crippling their work flow. Chinese companies are heeding the call as well, especially after Dell's politically motivated withdrawal from manufacturing in china. Then again, the top xeon processors have been banned from sale in China for many years. Together with the move towards gpu powered ai data centers, and the growing realization of windows on ARM, it has been a triple whammy for Intel, as its rug is pulled on its most profitable ecosystems (servers and mobile content creation). So yes, Intel has been hurt by toxic American politics, but its problems go deeper than that. Intel's business model hasn't kept up with the shifting sands of the chip market and is in danger of obsolescence.

Question: Do you agree with Italy's decision to withdraw from China's Belt and Road Initiative, citing concerns about consistency with alliances and European Union values? Why or why not?
Answer: The BRI is more than a decade old. Currently, >150 nations have expressed interest in boarding the BRI train, and participation at meetings in Beijing have been increasing. Now, the world is ~200 nations. 150 is practically every state in the global South (or the third world). Almost every state in the global North is absent. Italy was the odd first world duck swimming in waters teeming with the “poorer relations”. It has chosen to withdraw, rationalizing the decision as values-driven. That is ok, because Italy is sovereign, and it takes two to clap. However, it will lose real projects that are hard-to-replace bargains, which could have helped Italy’s connectivity and economic growth. And China is ok with that. There is more than enough business and projects to explore with 150 partners, way more than China has the resources for. Earlier projects nearing completion/handover are the perfect advertisement, especially as they drive economic growth and bring prosperity to underserved populations, repeating what has happened throughout China. This will hammer home the fact the Chinese are here to stay, and are fully capable of delivering on agreed terms. Italy is what, 60m? The global south is 7b, a >100x multiple. Italy gets to demonstrate solidarity and exemplary values, while China doesn’t lose sleep over “lost business”. Looks like a win-win. Note: The I in BRI is short for Initiative. It isn’t an alliance or bloc. This is merely a gathering of nations to coordinate and propose infrastructure projects that increase CONNECTIVITY between destinations, and it can be domestic or cross-border in scope.

Taiwan remained a colony of Japan till 1945, when Japan surrendered control of Taiwan as part of the peace settlement, in accordance with the Cairo Declaration of 1943, and the Potsdam Declaration of 1945. The 1951 Treaty of San Francisco officially renounced Japan's treaty rights to Korea, Formosa (Taiwan) and the Pescadores and Hong Kong. If Korea was returned to the Korean people and Hong Kong to the British (as a colony) post-WWII, what makes Taiwan special? History is firmly on China’s side. The answer, as always, is American hegemony forcefully keeping the question alive. Taiwan remains the day-old chick stuffed back into its shell, because Taiwan is more useful as an ambiguous unhatched egg. No chirping allowed, lest it upsets the peace, unless, of course, America wants to, from time to time. On to the 21st century status quo. EVERY COUNTRY IN THE UN subscribes to the One China policy. In other words, NO COUNTRY recognizes both the ROC and the PRC diplomatically. Today, only 11 states, comprising less than 0.5% of the poorest and most isolated humanity remain holdouts, choosing Taipei instead of Beijing. These 11 states (Belize, Eswatini, Guatemala, Haiti, Marshall Islands, Palau, Paraguay, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Tuvalu) are all—without exception—tied at the umbilical to American largess and patronage. Ever since Taiwan lost the China seat at the UN in 1971, it hasn’t been a member of the UN, not even observer status. And when Taiwanese leaders drop by Washington, they do not fly direct. The trips are framed as stopovers from diplomatic visits to Belize or Guatemala. Taiwan is not a country. Palestine is. It is high time we end the terrible iniquity both peoples have suffered for over a century.

Question: Why are the Chinese claiming they are the oldest civilization, when they didn’t even exist when languages were developed? The Chinese lasted only 2,000 years. How did they maintain that long?
Answer: Well, America is the flagbearer of western civilization and it's all of 250 years old. And where did western civilization originate? Modern day middle-east/Mediterranean. America is an ocean away, but it spells in the Latin alphabet, and prints “in God we trust” on its currency. Clearly, western civilization is unbroken, because it can be traced from the time of the ancient sumerians, Egyptians and Persians, as recorded in the Bible. In fact, the way we tell time today is based on a recorded event in the bible: the birth of Jesus. Hence it is AD 2024 today. Anno Domini, Latin for “in the year of our lord”. But is it continuous, in the sense that today's Americans share cultural and historical commonality with others that also identify as western and those that came before them? The modern American may read Tacitus, quote Plato, and study machiavelli, but he doesn't identify as a Roman, Greek or Italian. The refrain “it's all Greek to me” is illuminating. In other words, western civilization share a loosely linked pool of knowledge, but what sets the westerner apart is still geography and DNA. After all, North Africa and the Middle East have suffered massive destruction in recent years despite being the cradle of western civilization. China is different. The fossil and DNA record clearly show modern Chinese are descended from paleolithic ancestors who settled and called it home. Elements of Neolithic culture found their way into the earliest xia and shang dynasties, including burial practices and cultural wares. Chinese writing can be traced to the oracle bones of the Shang, and character evolution remains a topic for active scholarship. There was a period of fragmentation during the long decline of the zhou in the spring-autumn and warring states, but qin unification consolidated Chinese block writing. It has remained a consistent whole for the past 2,200 years. The answer to “what it means to be Chinese” is rooted in continuity. History, culture, language, philosophy, the arts, technology, even governance and politics. Take for example the genealogy of confucius, which has been continuously maintained over 2,500 years tracing more than 80 generations, the world's longest extant record of human pedigree. There are over 2 million living descendants registered, with the estimated total well in excess of 3 million. Similarly, an educated Chinese youth today can visit the Shandong museum and read Sun Tzu's art of war off 2,200 year-old bamboo strips written during the Han dynasty. You can't do that with spelled languages. Even Shakespeare's prose is unwieldy to the point of being unreadable because a 4-century gap separates modern English from the romance of Shakespearean times. Chinese is drawn, not spelled. To be continued…

Question: Russia T72 tanks have destroyed the US M1A1 tanks in Ukraine war. Why have the US military technologies no match to Russian military technologies in the world?
Answer: That’s the wrong way to think about things. War isn’t about one tank vs. another in a one-on-one duel. War is about pitting one doctrine against the other. In modern warfare, that means combined arms, the system of systems integration of networked sensors, comms to deliver effective fire control and battlefield management. Then again, the T72 today is a far cry from the T72 of gulf war days. It has stabilized sights, can shoot on the move and uses upgraded ammo. The armor is also up-to-date. If an M1 meets a T72 today one on one, neither is a sitting duck. But it’s hard to pick a winner either. It depends on who gets to target and shoot first, the geometry of engagement, and of course, tactics and implementation. However, tank battles today are very different, because the doctrine has to be rewritten for the presence of drones, and drone countermeasures, as well as man-portable anti-tank missiles. Personally, I think the days of the big gun on tracked turret is numbered, with smaller, autonomous drones/robots/vehicles taking over.

Question: A rhetoric has emerged recently in some Western countries, which claims that China's comparative strength, or its economy, is peaking. What's the arguments for the so-called "Peak China"? How do you view it?
Answer: Peak China is simply a superimposition of late 80s/90s Japan onto today’s China. Popping asset bubble, shrinking and aging population, debt troubles, FDI drop, sanctions, dehumanization, stock market crash… The whole nine yards. I won’t bother with a flyby, because the Zeihans and Pettises of the world are doing a much better job pumping the collapse. In 2001, when China first ascended the WTO after a decades-long negotiation process, “a billion pairs of socks for an airliner” was still a popular refrain in the Chinese consciousness. 2001 isn’t too long ago. It was the year 9.11 happened, and also the year the forever war OF terror began. In 2024, this is what a modern Chinese factory looks like. Rows and rows of robots churning out thousands dollar battery packs like clockwork, driven by high speed networks, multiple sensors and AI-assisted fault-tolerant control. In 2001, I didn’t remember seeing any Chinese booths at the Singapore Air Show. Today, there are military and commercial offerings aplenty, including the C919, China’s answer to the narrowbody dominance of the A320 and B737. I have not checked but according to friends, BYD is able to begin risk production in its foreign factories within 12–18 months of the lease being signed, and ramp up to full production within 18 months of operation. BYD’s EV production is a radically different model to the Japanese and German ICE lines, and the progress is breathtaking, particularly the upstream control/access to tools and raw materials. In telecoms, Huawei is deploying 5.5G networks, with 10x the speed of 5G, with 5.5G modems on the device side playing catchup. Qualcomm may find itself licensing Huawei designs if it isn’t careful to keep up. Huawei has patents that cover the entire stack from server, network to device. There is immense potential of bandwidth enabling revolutions in industry and autonomous self-driving. Huawei’s comeback Mate 60 is selling very well, affecting Apple’s China shipments, down 30% yoy. The P70 is also attracting lots of attention pre-release. How much of the lost 200 million shipped volume will Huawei reclaim this year? On to chips. There are many fabs under construction today, from legacy to advanced nodes. China will make half the world’s chip by 2030, and conceivably becoming a net chip exporter within the next decade. This from a position of spending more on chip import than oil recently. China has achieved commercial availability of the world’s first gas-cooled 4th gen nuclear power plant, after passing years of stringent grid testing. The rest of the competition don’t even have a test reactor today, so the Chinese lead is a good 10–15 years. Can you imagine a world where the global south (or the 150 countries in the BRI) enjoy pockets of technology that is more affordable and better yet, cutting edge wrt the global north? That day is coming, if not the 2030s, then certainly the 2040s. That’s Chinese democratization for you. Whatever you think of the Chinese, they are just getting started.

Question: Latest data showed that China's GDP expanded 5.0% year on year in the first half of 2024. What can you tell from this data?
Answer: Well, it means the policy targets are being met. The Chinese PM’s day in the spotlight is his annual progress report during the two meetings in Beijing, a national gathering of China’s entire parliament, the world’s largest. During the session, the Premier, who is No. 2 behind the General Secretary/President, will also announce the GDP growth target. China has always met the target, other than during covid. It is probably the only economy in the world to provide such forecast, all the more remarkable because the numbers have been reliably met for decades. That is why big business love China, because the forecast removes a lot of guesswork from risk models. Li Qiang announced a 5% target for 2024. The data suggests it will be met, despite weakness in multiple sectors both domestic and foreign. China is juggling a severe asset bubble pop, driven by systemic changes in real estate. The heady days of the past 3–4 decades are not coming back. Now, asset depreciation typically lead to balance sheet recessions, as Japan showed. That is why America reacted the way it did during the GFC, informed by the Japan lesson. But China is a different beast. No fiscal or monetary elephant gun for covid, or the asset bubble popped by Beijing. At least none on the profligate scale of first world economies. China has insulated itself from the ravages of war, pestilence, and more recently, inflation. Instead, the Yuan has merely weakened 10% from its long-term average of 6.8 yuan to the dollar. China has plenty left in the policy toolbox to support economic growth. In fact, there is an argument to be made the government isn’t doing enough to alleviate youth unemployment, among other ills in the economy. The data points to deep reform in the Chinese economy, as well as a pivot away from first world markets. Domestically, the government can control the pace, but elsewhere, Chinese speed cannot be replicated. What is clear though, as BRI projects come online, is the added connectivity become strong drivers of trade growth, as previously underserved markets plug into the giant China supply chain, the factory of the world. Witness the spectacular growth in Central Asia, and in time, the Middle East and Mediterranean, from the -stans to Pakistan/Iran, from Russia into Europe proper. If I were an investor, I’d take a close look at Greece, Turkey and Hungary/Serbia as new gatekeepers to Western Europe. Check back in 2030. Epoch-making change is happening in the westward shift of East Asia. It is the Asian century, and Eurasia is being remade, right before our eyes. And yes, Russia is Asian, decisively so.
